item.title: CNMI mayors unite in strong opposition to proposed seabed mining
item.description: The mayors of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands have issued a unified statement opposing proposed seabed mining activity near the Marianas, following a federal notice announcing a mineral lease sale for offshore areas located 57 miles from Saipan and 47 miles from Guam. item.content:encoded:
The mayors of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands have issued a unified statement opposing proposed seabed mining activity near the Marianas, following a federal notice announcing a mineral lease sale for offshore areas located 57 miles from Saipan and 47 miles from Guam.

The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management on Aug. 17 released a notice for a December mineral lease sale covering large tracts of the Pacific seabed. The proposed lease area, while not within CNMI territorial waters, sits close enough to the islands to raise concerns among local leaders about potential environmental and economic impacts.

In a joint letter dated Sept. 10, the mayors of Saipan, Tinian and Aguiguan, Rota, and the Northern Islands said the CNMI has received “a serious lack of clear and reliable information” about the consequences of seabed mining. They noted that no comprehensive environmental impact assessments, scientific studies, or long‑term monitoring plans have been provided to demonstrate how deep‑sea ecosystems would be protected.

“Our ocean is central to the livelihood, food security, and cultural heritage of our people,” the mayors wrote. They warned that seabed mining “poses a significant risk of permanent damage to these fragile ecosystems, with consequences that could last for generations.”

The mayors also questioned the absence of any clear economic benefit to the CNMI, saying federal agencies have not explained how mining activities would create jobs, generate revenue, or provide long‑term value for the islands. “Without such assurances, it is unacceptable to place our natural resources at risk,” they said.

Another major concern is the lack of meaningful consultation with local governments and residents. The mayors said decisions that could permanently affect CNMI waters “must be made with full public participation, not without it.”

The letter, signed by Saipan Mayor Ramon “RB” Camacho, Tinian and Aguiguan Mayor Edwin P. Aldan, Rota Mayor Aubry M. Hocog, and Northern Islands Mayor Valentino Taisacan, urges BOEM to halt any advancement of seabed mining until full environmental studies, economic analyses, and community consultations are completed and made public.

“Protecting our ocean today protects the future of our people, our economy, and our islands,” they wrote.

Their opposition comes as Pacific governments, environmental groups, and regional organizations continue to scrutinize deep‑sea mining proposals across the region, citing risks to biodiversity, fisheries, and cultural waters.

item.title: Prutehi Guåhan and UOG Social Work Student Alliance host ‘Deep Sea Mining 101’
item.description: Prutehi Guåhan, in collaboration with the University of Guam’s Social Work Student Alliance, is screening a short documentary titled “ Deep Sea Mining 101 .” The showing will be from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. Sept. 30 at the UOG Fine Arts Theater.
item.content:encoded:
Prutehi Guåhan, in collaboration with the University of Guam’s Social Work Student Alliance, is screening a short documentary titled “ Deep Sea Mining 101 .”

The showing will be from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. Sept. 30 at the UOG Fine Arts Theater.

According to Prutehi Guåhan, the event is being held to educate and engage the community on the basics of deep-sea mining. Participants will discuss the politics and potential consequences of deep-sea mining in the Mariana Islands. Naek Flores, executive director of Prutehi Guåhan, said the federal government has announced the lease sale to begin in December for the areas flanking both sides of the Marianas. Flores said that the efforts of Prutehi Guåhan and organizations like UOG will help engage the community with what is being attempted in the oceans of the Marianas. “Unfortunately, Guam has been locked out of the comment period, and so we need to come together, have these conversations, talk to our elected officials, speak to the leadership in the CNMI, and also find ways to connect and collaborate with other Pacific communities going through these same risks,” Flores said.

On Aug. 17, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management issued a notice for a mineral lease sale near the Marianas. While a notice, as well as a request for comment, was sent to Gov. David Apatang of the CNMI, the same opportunity was not given to Guam. On Sept. 15, Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero wrote to the Trump administration requesting that Guam also have a voice in the process. The proposed lease area is situated 57 miles from Saipan and 47 miles from Guam.

Prutehi Guåhan has hosted several events around deep-sea mining. In 2025 and 2026, they hosted two comment-writing workshops with attorneys from Earth Justice to help community members prepare comments on the proposals for deep-sea mining in the Marianas. Additionally, they have also hosted protests in Guam and Saipan.

This is the first of two screenings Prutehi Guåhan plans for the community. Their second will be in November at the Guam Community College.

item.title: Storm damage, teacher losses push CNMI PSS into deepening crisis
item.description: Acting Commissioner Jacquilene Che told Rotary Club members Tuesday that the CNMI public school system is facing its most severe fiscal pressures in three decades, with storm‑damaged campuses, staffing shortages, and shrinking federal aid straining daily operations. Che previously served as the Public School System federal programs officer before being appointed acting commissioner in June 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Acting Commissioner Jacquilene Che told Rotary Club members Tuesday that the CNMI public school system is facing its most severe fiscal pressures in three decades, with storm‑damaged campuses, staffing shortages, and shrinking federal aid straining daily operations.

Che previously served as the Public School System federal programs officer before being appointed acting commissioner in June 2026.

Che said PSS opened all 20 public schools on Aug. 18 even as many campuses remained in disrepair, with broken roofs, damaged windows, and facilities still awaiting FEMA support. Kagman Elementary and Chacha Oceanview only recently returned to full‑day schedules after weeks of dual sessions that split students into morning and afternoon shifts.

She said the system’s financial instability deepened after the expiration of American Rescue Plan Act funding, leaving PSS with budget deficits and fewer resources to sustain operations. Since January, PSS has lost 10% of its workforce — including one‑third of its classroom teachers — prompting the reassignment of central office staff with teaching backgrounds back into schools.

Che said she intends to restore a full five‑day instructional week by early October, replacing Monday closures with federally funded tutoring, counseling, meals, and wellness programming. She also highlighted rising student trauma tied to economic hardship, domestic stress, and years of disruptions from Typhoon Yutu, COVID‑19, and austerity measures.

PSS is launching trauma‑informed wellness hubs to support students facing depression, anxiety, and food insecurity.

Che asked Rotarians to help repair damaged school bus stops across Saipan, Tinian, and Rota, noting that many are unsafe and exposed to heavy rain and heat. She said the Department of Public Works lacks sufficient funding to address the issue.

Despite the challenges, Che said she remains hopeful. “Our students are resilient, they are capable, and they deserve nothing less than our best,” she said.

item.title: Judge considers restoring journalists' access to White House after Trump's ban
item.description: Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR A federal judge appeared inclined to order the White House to restore — at least temporarily — the press passes of journalists for CNN, Politico and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC).
item.content:encoded:
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR

A federal judge appeared inclined to order the White House to restore — at least temporarily — the press passes of journalists for CNN, Politico and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC).

On Wednesday afternoon, U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, held an emergency hearing after the news outlets filed a lawsuit seeking to undo the ban.

In his introductory remarks, Kelly said it appeared the White House had violated the news outlets' constitutional right of due process — which was set out in previous court decisions — when it abruptly blocked the access of journalists who held permanent credentials to work in the building.

Theodore J. Boutrous, a lawyer representing the three news outlets, said the White House ban took place " without a semblance of due process."

He also argued that the move was in violation of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's First Amendment rights and called it a form of retaliation for their coverage of the president, adding that it was "probably the clearest case in history" of viewpoint discrimination.

In threatening to ban the news outlets on Friday, Trump had told reporters at the White House, "They purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration."

Boutrous further contended the news organizations were suffering irreparable harm by being locked out of the White House at a time of war, and on the eve of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.

" The constitutional violation is against the public interest," he said.

Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik, on the other hand, argued that access to the White House was a "privilege," not a right. He also cited national security concerns as a reason for the continued ban. In its legal filings, the department had included White House letters to the three news organizations taking issue with stories on a variety of topics, including construction of a "top secret" bunker under the White House ballroom, talks with Iran and whether there were "very bad" vibes at the recent Republican convention in Dallas.

Boutrous pushed back on the claim, asserting that the first mention of national security came only days after the ban was imposed.

" I guess the light bulb went off and they all decided 'Start talking about national security,'" Boutrous said.

Kelly did not rule from the bench, adding that he will consider both sides and make a decision as soon as possible.

item.title: Trump and Xi meet at moment of global consequence
item.description: Updated September 24, 2026 at 8:04 AM ChST BEIJING/WASHINGTON — Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in the United States on Wednesday evening for his first state visit in 11 years, opening high-stakes talks with President Trump at a pivotal moment for both men.
item.content:encoded:
Updated September 24, 2026 at 8:04 AM ChST

BEIJING/WASHINGTON — Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in the United States on Wednesday evening for his first state visit in 11 years, opening high-stakes talks with President Trump at a pivotal moment for both men.

It is the second time the leaders are meeting this year after the Beijing summit in May, when they agreed to build a more stable bilateral relationship.

Both leaders are trying to shore up power at home. For Trump, the visit comes just over a month before the midterm elections, and for Xi, preparations for an all-important Party Congress start when he returns to Beijing.

But despite both countries projecting a willingness to build what China has dubbed a relationship of "constructive strategic stability," fierce negotiations over weighty subjects such as AI and trade are underway.

"Under the water, the Chinese seem to have done a lot of kicking lately. And you know, if we have to, we'll kick back," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview in July.

Trump has frequently spoken warmly about how he was treated during his recent visit to China, which included pageantry and a state banquet at Beijing's Great Hall of the People.

One of the banquet attendees, Wu Xinbo, who directs the American Studies center at Shanghai's Fudan University, said it was the warmest he had seen in the U.S.-China relations in years.

But since then, Wu said, things have been more "fragile."

"In the last several months, the U.S. has continued to contain and pressure China in economic, technological [and] people-to-people exchanges," he said.

For example, the U.S. imposed extra tariffs on Chinese exports over forced labor claims, and the Pentagon added Chinese tech giants on a military blacklist . The Federal Communications Commission banned new imports of Chinese humanoid robots and robot dogs over national security concerns.

Ups and downs are to be expected in a relationship as complicated as the U.S. and China's, said international studies professor Zhang Yun at Nanjing University.

The key is to build high-level channels to deal with problems as they emerge and "mitigate the negative impacts," he said.

Zhang said Taiwan, tech and trade are high on Xi's agenda this trip. Discussions on the wars in Iran and Ukraine, plus tensions along the Korean peninsula, are also expected.

The U.S. is expected to reciprocate the high level of pomp and circumstance for Xi regardless of the tough negotiations expected — and Trump has publicly held Xi in high regard.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that the two countries are still negotiating the potential extension of a rare earths truce that would ensure continued flow of Chinese rare earth products for the U.S.

China dominates the refining of rare earths and other critical minerals that are important to manufacture a range of products, from cellphones to weapons.

However, American officials have complained that China has not upheld its end of the bargain. NPR reporting shows that mutual distrust scuppered an offer from Beijing to extend the rare earths truce to the end of Trump's term, in January 2029.

Trump and Xi are also expected to talk about AI governance.

China has "been trying to figure out, in talking to the United States, what kind of so-called guardrails or controls can be put on artificial intelligence," said Rose Gottemoeller , a former NATO official who attends regular dialogues on nuclear proliferation with retired Chinese military officials.

"So it's a combination nowadays of the older issues related to nuclear stability and new issues related to new technology," she said.

China is interested in imposing safety measures, according to Zhang, but he said there is a lot of "mistrust" between the U.S. and China on the proposed solutions.

In their previous meetings, Xi has repeatedly emphasized to Trump that Taiwan, a self-governing island Beijing claims as its own, is a red line and if mishandled could put the U.S.-China relations in "jeopardy." Trump told reporters later that he was not interested in a war thousands of miles away.

"Let's see if the United States can make [a] clearer statement opposing Taiwan independence," said Zhang.

This spring, the Trump administration paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. Experts say Xi is expected to press Trump to maintain this momentum when he sits down with Trump on Thursday.

On Wednesday, as Xi departed for the U.S., China's state news agency published a statement from the country's cabinet-like State Council excoriating Taiwan's president, Lai Ching-te. Lai is despised by Beijing, which suspects he is trying to lead Taiwan to declare formal independence.

"The most important issue that the Chinese always raise in preparation for these high-level visits is the topic of Taiwan," says William Klein , acting deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing until 2021.

Trump and Xi also agreed to create trade and investment boards back in May. Among the discussions is a reciprocal tariff reduction framework on products worth $30 billion or more.

China is expected to announce purchases of American agricultural products, and the U.S. is expected to announce tariff reductions on what are called 4A consumer goods, which include footwear and apparel, according to two people in the U.S.-China business community who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

However, no details of who will be on either trade or investment boards have been announced yet.

item.title: Iran's president gives a rare wartime speech at the U.N.
item.description: Iran's president gave a rare speech in New York by a country at war with the United States on Wednesday, a day after President Trump threatened from the same podium to "annihilate" Iran. "Yesterday the United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the United Nations General Assembly.
item.content:encoded:
Iran's president gave a rare speech in New York by a country at war with the United States on Wednesday, a day after President Trump threatened from the same podium to "annihilate" Iran.

"Yesterday the United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the United Nations General Assembly.

He proceeded to hold up a portrait of the late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei , who was killed on the first day of U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. He then held up photos of children he said were the victims of a U.S. bombing of an Iranian school.

Speaking at the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, President Trump said he faced a big decision: Make a deal with Iran that lets them rebuild or " annihilate the Islamic Republic ." He also reiterated that he would not allow Iran to develop a nuclear weapon.

Trump later said U.S. officials had met with Iranians for three hours. U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told NPR's Morning Edition on Wednesday that the administration is "internalizing what they brought to the table."

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said on social media that an exchange of messages between Iran and the U.S. had taken place with Qatar as mediator. He said Iran's conditions included halting U.S. hostilities, an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and the release of Iranian funds.

Pezeshkian denied at the U.N. that Iran wanted a nuclear weapon but refused limitations on the country's civilian nuclear program. He also expressed a willingness to negotiate.

"It must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," he said.

item.title: A Catholic media star will be beatified in St. Louis, moving a step closer to sainthood
item.description: (RNS) — In 1953, Lucille Ball, the star of the hit show "I Love Lucy," was up for an Emmy for "Most Outstanding Personality." She lost — to a Catholic bishop, Fulton J. Sheen.
item.content:encoded:
(RNS) — In 1953, Lucille Ball, the star of the hit show "I Love Lucy," was up for an Emmy for "Most Outstanding Personality."

She lost — to a Catholic bishop, Fulton J. Sheen.

"I feel it is time I pay tribute to my four writers — Matthew, Mark, Luke and John," Sheen reportedly quipped as he accepted the award.

This Thursday, the bishop who charmed millions while scrawling theological concepts on a blackboard for his show "Life Is Worth Living" will come one step closer to being declared a saint. His beatification, which comes after the Vatican found that he lived a life of "heroic virtue" and that his intercession was responsible for a miracle, leaves him one miracle shy of sainthood.

Sheen's beatification Mass will take place in St. Louis' former NFL Stadium, the Dome at America's Center, and will be presided over by Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, a media star of his own in the Philippines. It will also be broadcast by Catholic media giant EWTN and livestreamed on the YouTube channel of the Diocese of Peoria, Illinois, the diocese where Sheen was ordained.

For Sheen's fans and the team promoting his sainthood cause, the beatification is a moment to celebrate his enduring impact on evangelization, Catholic media and U.S. spirituality.

"One of his lasting legacies," said Bishop Louis Tylka of Peoria, Ill., the promoter of Sheen's cause for canonization, "is the example and invitation for us to, like him, deepen our friendship with Jesus each and every day by being people of prayer, and in particular, praying in front of the Blessed Sacrament."

Tylka said Sheen's example of praying for an hour a day before the Eucharist — a practice he called the Holy Hour — helped popularize the devotion.

Sheen was born May 8, 1895, in El Paso, Illinois, and was ordained a priest in 1919. He taught theology and philosophy at the Catholic University of America from 1926 to 1950. After Sheen's time in the Archdiocese of New York, he was appointed Bishop of Rochester in 1966 and then was named an archbishop in 1969.

In 1930, he began hosting a Sunday night radio show, called "The Catholic Hour," that reportedly drew 4 million weekly listeners through national syndication on NBC Radio Network. In 1951, after he became auxiliary bishop in New York, he began hosting his TV show, "Life Is Worth Living."

Lonnie Carter, an award-winning playwright, remembers being "captivated" by the Tuesday night program as a child. "The bishop had a wicked sense of humor," and a following that extended beyond his fellow Catholics to his Jewish friends, said Carter.

Carter later met Sheen at the wedding of Sheen's niece and Carter's Marquette University classmate. "I found him to be present, dignified of course, humble in a sort of arrogant way and devilishly handsome," Carter told Religion News Service.

Carter, inspired by the upcoming beatification, has written a one-man play about Sheen, where Carter mixes excerpts from one real Sheen sermon with imagined sermons written by Carter on topics like football and poetry.

Organizers expect 50,000 people to attend the beatification Mass on Thursday — many with their own memories of Sheen and his show.

In the Diocese of Peoria, Sheen's prayer life has also inspired lay Catholics. Bonnie and Travis Engstrom had the custom of putting each of their children under the patronage of a saint, but when Bonnie was pregnant with her son James Fulton in 2010, she began to watch recordings of Sheen's shows on YouTube, and they decided to pray for Sheen's intercession.

"He was so intelligent, but I felt like he had a way of taking really complex philosophy and political thought" to "break it down" for the masses, said Bonnie Engstrom.

During Engstrom's pregnancy, "everything pointed to a healthy baby," she said. James would be her third planned home birth. But when the midwife handed James to her, " he was completely limp" and a "bluish-gray" color.

As the midwife began CPR, her husband performed an emergency baptism and her friend left to call 911, Engstrom was in "a state of shock." She said, "I just remember sitting on the floor and not really being able to process anything, but I remember thinking in my head, 'Fulton Sheen, Fulton Sheen, Fulton Sheen.'" Engstrom said it was like when you're walking next to a friend, and you trip and then call out their name.

James' heart didn't beat at their home or in the ambulance or even when he first arrived at the emergency room. Days later, an attending physician in the neonatal intensive care unit added up the minutes James had been without a heart beat — and to the doctor's disbelief, it had been one hour and one minute.

"I think very much so that Bishop Sheen made a Holy Hour, and when that Holy Hour was over, that was when Jesus Christ brought James back to life," she said. "It was at 61 minutes, not 59," she explained.

James is now a healthy 16-year-old and the team manager for his high school's freshmen football team. He and his family will be present at the beatification.

Engstrom said watching the Vatican's meticulous process for verifying her son's miracle — that it did not have a medical explanation and that Sheen was responsible — has reassured her faith in the Church.

" I now know how thoroughly that has been investigated, and there's a lot of rigor that goes into it," she said.
